agreements.title: Five Agreements · practise a helpful choice
agreements.intro: The Four Agreements come from don Miguel Ruiz; the fifth is shared with don Jose Ruiz. Explore one idea at a time using your own words, acting or drawing. You may pass.
agreements.prep: Later lesson · about 60 minutes. Revisit the belonging commitment (5); explore the five ideas and infographic (10); model Watch a replay (10); rehearse Your scene with speaking or drawing options (15); discuss and revise (10); choose a concrete action and exit check (10). Use the physical cards, plain paper and pencils. These screens are classroom adaptations, not reproductions of the commercial deck. Students may question the ideas; shared spiritual beliefs are not required. Use the on-screen infographic and scenarios without video. Optional author media needs a teacher preview. Feelings are valid, and harm still needs adult support and repair.

sources.label: The Fifth Agreement · author-site excerpt
sources.description: Teacher background for listening and questioning. Classroom prompt: how can we hear someone out and still check whether a claim is accurate?

sources.label: Understanding the Fifth Agreement · Karla Ruiz
sources.description: Additional teacher background. This philosophical reading is more abstract than the classroom cards; use the game-rule example to make the discussion concrete.

cards.title: Start here · four ideas, then a fifth
cards.prompt: What promise could you make to yourself that helps our class?
cards.action: An agreement is a choice we try to practise. Listen to an idea from the cards. Tell a partner what it might look like during work or play.
cards.model: “When I disagree, I can ask a question before deciding someone is wrong.”
cards.teacher: Introduce don Miguel Ruiz as the author of The Four Agreements and don Jose Ruiz as co-author of The Fifth Agreement. These screens offer our own classroom examples. Students can question the ideas and suggest improvements. The books include spiritual beliefs; our activity explores communication and choices without requiring shared beliefs. Do not present these books as the teachings of all Indigenous peoples.

cards.title: 1 · Use words with care
cards.prompt: How can you be honest and kind at the same time?
cards.action: A partner makes an unexpected chess move. Practise a useful response.
cards.model: “I think that piece moves differently. Shall we check the rule together?”
cards.teacher: Explain impeccable as taking care with what you say. Honesty does not require insults; kindness does not require pretending. Ask which words help someone learn.
cards.discussion: How could you repair things after your words hurt someone?

cards.title: 2 · Remember your worth
cards.prompt: Someone’s reaction does not decide your value.
cards.action: You invite someone to play; they choose a different game. Suggest two possible reasons.
cards.model: “They may want a different game today. I can feel disappointed and still ask someone else.”
cards.teacher: Avoid telling children not to feel hurt. This idea never excuses exclusion, harassment or discrimination. Help students seek support and address harm; do not place responsibility for mistreatment on the person harmed.
cards.discussion: Can you feel hurt and still remember that you matter? What help could you ask for?

cards.title: 3 · Ask before deciding
cards.prompt: What did you notice? What are you guessing?
cards.action: Your blue pencil is missing. A classmate has a blue pencil. Ask a question without accusing.
cards.model: “I can’t find my blue pencil. Have you seen it?”
cards.teacher: The matching colour is an observation, not proof of ownership. Invite a second possible explanation. Do not use a real missing item or name a student.
cards.discussion: How is something you saw different from a story you guessed?

cards.title: 4 · Choose a useful next step
cards.prompt: What could your best effort look like today?
cards.action: Your display page needs work, and you feel tired. Choose one manageable improvement.
cards.model: “I will add a clear title, then ask for help with one sentence.”
cards.teacher: Effort varies with energy, access and support. Best does not mean perfect, fastest or doing everything. A break, assistance or a smaller task can be a useful choice.
cards.discussion: Could asking for help or taking a break be part of doing your best? Why?

cards.title: 5 · Listen and check
cards.prompt: How can you listen respectfully without believing every claim?
cards.action: Someone says a game rule changed. What could you check before changing how everyone plays?
cards.model: “I hear that you learned a different rule. Let’s read the rule card together.”
cards.teacher: Fifth-agreement connection: be skeptical while learning to listen. Check the claim, not the person’s worth. Distinguish a factual claim from a feeling: listen to someone saying they feel hurt; do not demand that they prove their feeling.
cards.agreement: Be Skeptical, But Learn to Listen
cards.discussion: What is the difference between checking a claim and refusing to listen?

cards.title: Watch a replay
cards.prompt: A player says, “You always ruin the game!”
cards.action: Notice the change when we replace the accusation with a clear question.
cards.model: “I saw the piece move twice. Are we using a rule I don’t know? Can we check before the next turn?”
cards.teacher: Model both versions calmly with an imaginary partner. Do not invite students to perform exaggerated insults. Ask: what is observed, what was assumed, and what does the second version make possible? Several agreements can fit.

cards.title: Your scene · choose one
cards.prompt: A missing pencil. Different music choices. A mistake in a game. A display that needs another try.
cards.action: In pairs, choose a scene and an agreement. Prepare a 20–30 second helpful response. You may draw speech bubbles instead.
cards.model: Show the situation → make a helpful choice → explain the agreement.
cards.teacher: Allow about 10 minutes, but let ready pairs share sooner. Partners share speaking or drawing roles. Ask viewers to identify the choice and explain its effect; there is no single required answer.

cards.title: One choice for today
cards.prompt: What will you try while we work or play?
cards.action: Finish: “When ___ happens, I can ___.” Tell a partner or sketch your idea.
cards.model: “When I’m unsure about a rule, I can ask before accusing.”
cards.teacher: Look for one concrete action students can actually try. Ask what help they might need. A student may keep their response private. Revisit the choice after the next shared activity.

cards.title: Keep going · two ideas at once
cards.prompt: Two friends want different jobs on the classroom display.
cards.action: Try two possible agreements. Create a solution that gives both people a voice.
cards.model: “Let’s hear each idea, then divide the jobs or swap after ten minutes.”
cards.teacher: Optional extension, not an extra required task. Check whether students actually listen before offering the solution. Save NVC for its own substantial lesson.

poster.title: Start with an illustrated overview
poster.credit: The Four Agreements · summarized by Butterfly Dreamz
poster.alt: Butterfly Dreamz illustrated Four Agreements poster: use truthful and caring language; remember that others’ reactions do not define your worth; ask questions before drawing conclusions; make an effort suited to your circumstances.
poster.prompt: Choose one agreement. What could it look like during a game or group task?
poster.note: You can feel hurt and still know you matter. Ask for help with bullying or unfair treatment. Your best can include support and rest.

nvc.title: NVC · notice, feel, need, ask
nvc.intro: We can practise understanding one another when things are already going well.
nvc.prep: Later lesson · about 60 minutes using Marshall Rosenberg’s Nonviolent Communication approach. Revisit a belonging commitment and appreciation (5); model four parts (10); sort noticing from judging and explore feelings/needs (10); rehearse a request and response (10); practise the two-needs scenario, then replay (15); reflect and choose a next step (10). Use fictional situations, the on-screen word bank and optional cards from your own deck. Students may point, draw, speak, dictate or pass; listening never requires eye contact. The four-part sentence is a support, not a compulsory script. Adults set safety boundaries and intervene in harm; children do not have to negotiate access or unsafe behaviour.

cards.title: Start with appreciation
cards.prompt: What did someone do that helped you today?
cards.action: Use a real small kindness or the example. Say what happened and why it mattered.
cards.model: “When you made room at the game, I felt glad because being included matters to me.”
cards.teacher: About 3 minutes. No forced public praise, ranking of friends, or naming someone who did not help. This is a positive entry to observations, feelings and needs.

cards.title: Notice · feel · need · ask
cards.prompt: Say what happened, name a feeling, explain what matters, and ask for a doable action.
cards.action: Read the four parts together. Point to each part in the example.
cards.model: “When the music is loud, I feel distracted because I need concentration. Would you turn it down while I finish this?”
cards.teacher: Observation: music volume; feeling/state: distracted; need: concentration; request: lower volume during work. Model a natural shorter version too: “I’m finding it hard to focus. Could we lower the volume for ten minutes?”

cards.title: Notice without judging
cards.prompt: Which sentence describes something we could see or hear?
cards.action: Compare “You never let anyone talk” with “I started twice, and someone spoke before I finished.” Rewrite “You are selfish with supplies” using a fictional action you could observe.
cards.model: “The marker has stayed at your desk during our group task.” Then ask what happened; do not decide the person’s motive.
cards.teacher: Invite several observable versions. Avoid always/never. Feelings remain valid even when an observation needs checking.

cards.title: Find a feeling and a need
cards.prompt: Feelings: glad, worried, frustrated, calm, disappointed, curious. Needs: belonging, fairness, choice, rest, learning, space.
cards.action: A friend invites you into a game. Choose a feeling and a need that might fit. Another answer may also fit.
cards.model: “Maybe glad, because belonging matters.” Ask: “Does that fit, or is it something else?”
cards.teacher: Use these original short word banks or suitable cards. Feelings are not accusations: “ignored” can imply what another person did; help a child explore whether sad, lonely or frustrated fits, without correcting or dismissing their own wording.

cards.title: Try a clear request
cards.prompt: Two people reach for the same marker.
cards.action: With a partner, practise naming what happened and asking for a turn. Then swap roles.
cards.model: “We both reached for the blue marker. I feel impatient because I want to finish. Could I use it after your outline?”
cards.teacher: A request names an observable action. The other person can offer another plan. Do not require the full formula when a clear, respectful sentence works. Avoid demanding an apology or agreement.

cards.title: Listen, then respond
cards.prompt: What could you say if you are not ready to say yes?
cards.action: Respond to the marker request. Show that you heard the other person and offer a workable next step.
cards.model: “You want a turn to finish your picture. I need two more minutes. Would that work?”
cards.teacher: Listening does not require eye contact. Encourage a brief check of understanding rather than guessing motives. If repeated exclusion or intimidation appears, the adult intervenes; this is not a substitute for support.

cards.title: Two needs can both matter
cards.prompt: One group wants music to help them work. Another needs quiet to concentrate.
cards.action: In pairs, practise both voices. Each person names a possible feeling, a need and a doable request. Offer two plans. Swap voices or use speech bubbles, then replay after feedback.
cards.model: “I feel distracted with music playing because I need quiet. Could we try ten quiet minutes?” “I enjoy music, but I hear you need quiet. Could we keep the shared space quiet now and ask the teacher about another music time?”
cards.teacher: Allow 15 minutes for first attempt, feedback and replay. Needs are not a contest. A proposed strategy is not automatically a right or a workable accommodation. Adults ensure access; do not vote away someone’s necessary support. Check: observation, possible feeling, need, specific request, response that shows listening.

cards.title: Try it in our day
cards.prompt: Where could this help: games, music, shared supplies or outdoor play?
cards.action: Choose one moment. Practise a sentence or draw speech bubbles.
cards.model: “When the rules are read quickly, I feel unsure because I need clarity. Could we see one practice round?”
cards.teacher: Exit: identify one observation, feeling, need and request in your example. Ask what changed when both people were heard. Practise one part briefly across later group work; adults retain responsibility for removing barriers.

belonging.title: Who gets to belong?
belonging.intro: How do we build communities where people actually belong? Being invited is a start. Belonging means we can take part, contribute and feel part of the group.
belonging.prep: Monday: 30 minutes, 8:50–9:20. Use the six projector cards in order: 3 + 4 + 5 + 5 + 8 + 5 minutes. Read aloud; offer quiet thinking and pointing, speaking, drawing, writing or dictating. A partner may record an idea with permission. No devices or individual worksheets are required. Prepare one class chart with Person, Barrier and Redesign headings. Use fictional people; never ask a student to explain a disability or prove an access need. Do not simulate disabilities. Adults remain responsible for safe, meaningful access; inclusion is not a majority vote. Keep the other community lessons for later days.

cards.title: 1 · Notice, take responsibility, repair · 3 min
cards.prompt: When a choice leaves people out, we can change it.
cards.action: Listen to our teacher’s repair. Think quietly: what would need to change next time? You do not need to name anyone or share a private experience.
cards.model: “I chose Capture the Flag on the gravel field without checking that everyone could take part meaningfully. I am sorry. Planning for everyone is my responsibility. We will look at the barriers, change the activity and check whether the changes work.”
cards.teacher: Read this brief acknowledgement in your own voice. Do not seek forgiveness, identify anyone or ask the class to validate the apology. The next action, not a long explanation, models responsibility.
cards.discussion: Notice the problem → take responsibility → repair → change future practice.

cards.title: 2 · Invited or included? · 4 min
cards.prompt: What is the difference between being invited and actually belonging?
cards.action: Imagine a class chooses a game. Most can join easily. Some cannot take part fully because of the rules, equipment, space, movement, language or noise. Is it inclusive simply because everyone was invited? Think, then share an idea.
cards.model: An invitation does not remove a rule or space that blocks participation. A person belongs when they have a meaningful way to contribute to the shared activity.
cards.teacher: Take two or three ideas after quiet thinking. Read the scenario aloud. Keep discussion general. Do not assume the person wants a particular role or support.

cards.title: 3 · Person → Barrier → Redesign · 5 min
cards.prompt: What could we change about the activity or environment?
cards.action: PERSON: what does the fictional person want to do? BARRIER: what gets in the way? REDESIGN: what could change so they can take part in the same goal? Ask what works; do not guess someone’s abilities.
cards.model: Person: a player wants to help their team make decisions. Barrier: rules are explained once, quickly, over loud music. Redesign: pause the music, show the rules and model one round, with time to ask questions.
cards.teacher: Point to each heading on the class chart. Person means a participant’s goal and preferences, not a diagnosis. This adapts Barrier Detectives’ existing barrier-to-tool match.
cards.discussion: What is the barrier? Is our idea changing it, or asking the person to put up with it?

cards.title: 4 · Notice more than one barrier · 5 min
cards.prompt: Who can take part, and what might still get in the way?
cards.action: Choose one fictional case: a route has steps; answers must be long and handwritten; only fast speakers get heard; an event assumes every family shares one celebration. Name a barrier without naming a classmate.
cards.model: If only fast speakers are heard, build in thinking time and invite speech, pointing, drawing or a partner reading an idea with permission. Everyone can still contribute to the decision.
cards.teacher: Briefly gather barriers across movement, communication, sensory load, reading/writing, language, social rules, culture and less visible needs such as energy or pain. No one has to disclose a reason for a support. Use just one or two cases Monday; save the rest.
cards.discussion: How could someone share an idea without speaking to the whole class?

cards.title: 5 · Redesign together · 8 min
cards.prompt: How will your change make real participation possible?
cards.action: With a partner, choose one case. Say, point, sketch or dictate: “A person wants to ___. The barrier is ___. We could change ___.” Check that everyone can still help with the shared goal. Share one idea; improve it after feedback.
cards.model: For a team puzzle, put all clues at reachable stations on a clear route. Offer spoken and pictured clues. Players choose how to solve and communicate; the team needs everyone’s ideas. Check the route and choices before trying it.
cards.teacher: 2 minutes choose and think; 3 minutes partner redesign; 3 minutes share and revise. Meaningful participation is more than compulsory scorekeeping or watching. A role can be legitimate when chosen and valued; it cannot be the only option because of a barrier. Adults check safety and feasibility before a trial.
cards.discussion: How could we find out whether our change helped without putting someone on the spot?

cards.title: 6 · Make a commitment and check it · 5 min
cards.prompt: What will we change before our next shared activity?
cards.action: Finish together: “Before we ___, we will ___ so people can ___. We will check by ___.” Choose two practical actions and a check-back time. Give feedback aloud, by pointing, on a note or privately.
cards.model: “Before our next group activity, we will explain and model the task, check the space, and offer meaningful ways to contribute. Afterwards, we will ask what helped and what still needs changing.”
cards.teacher: Record two class actions on one chart. At the 2:00 activity/care block, check whether the actions are usable; do not promise a game. Revisit for 5 minutes at the next community lesson. Record changes, not names or diagnoses.
cards.discussion: Exit: “An invitation is not enough when ___. One change we could try is ___.”
